summary:
Moon park is an interactive application designed such as from students learning about lunar exploration to mission teams evaluating landing options can be utilized by anyone. It addresses a critical challenge at the Moon’s south pole, where changes in location or arrival date can affect sunlight availability and direct-to-Earth communication.

Users select a landing site and date by selecting a site from previous mission or even entering custom coordinates, explore Sun and Earth positions relative to the horizon, and compare scenarios through synchronized 3D views and timelines. These visualizations connect site selection with sunlight duration, solar elevation, and overlapping power and communication opportunities.

A 3D AI assistant provides two entry points. Users can describe a scenario in everyday language to configure their exploration, or ask questions at any point to understand the displayed conditions and available controls.

Our prototype uses simplified geometry to demonstrate this workflow. By bringing spatial context, time, comparison, and accessible explanations together, the project aims to support shared understanding across science and engineering teams while making lunar mission planning approachable for the public.
details:
Moon Park is an interactive lunar landing site navigator that helps users explore how location and arrival time affect modeled sunlight and direct Earth visibility. Users can choose a location from the catalogue, enter custom lunar coordinates, or explore named mission targets. They can set an arrival date, delay, stay duration, and observer height, then generate a scenario and inspect its results in a 3D lunar environment. It is designed such that it could be used by a college student or people actually doing mission planning.

The tool brings several planning views together: a lunar globe, a location map, a terrain horizon, and a timeline of visibility. It highlights solar elevation, total sunlight, direct Earth visibility, shared visibility windows, and sampled times to the next visibility change. Users can compare sites or dates, examine schedule alternatives, and use the conversational AI assistant to ask questions or describe a scenario in natural language. AI guidance helps interpret the interface and prepare supported requests; the local scientific engine performs the visibility calculations.

Moon Park addresses the challenge of making lunar site and date comparisons faster to understand. Instead of requiring users to assemble information from separate tools, it presents the scenario, visual context, key metrics, and limitations together. This can help students, educators, and mission-planning teams see why a small change in location or schedule may alter visibility, and compare alternatives when plans change.

The project combines JavaScript and Three.js for the interactive interface and 3D views, a local Node.js service for application and calculation jobs, and Python scientific routines for terrain and observation processing. It uses NASA lunar imagery and topography, lunar and spacecraft ephemeris resources, and supplied 3D models for visualization.

The design considers custom-coordinate entry, multiple-site and date comparisons, accessibility across experience levels, responsive layouts, source traceability, uncertainty, terrain coverage, and the Moon’s airless horizon. Results are modeled decision support: visibility does not establish landing safety, electrical power, radio-link performance, thermal survival, or mission feasibility.
